strengths: The paper proposes a clear and useful sampler parameterization: a generalized multistep update using all previous states and velocities, with learned residual corrections around theoretically derived DPM-Solver++ coefficients. The initialization is sensible and preserves a strong conventional solver before optimization.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering six datasets, pixel-space and latent diffusion, class-conditional generation, and Stable Diffusion text-to-image generation across several low-NFE budgets.

Results are particularly convincing at four NFEs. For example, GAS improves over S4S from 10.63 to 7.86 FID on FFHQ and from 6.52 to 4.48 on AFHQv2. The comparison between GS and GAS also provides evidence that adversarial training helps in the hardest low-NFE regimes.
The paper evaluates relevant solver-optimization baselines, including LD3, S4S, GITS, and DMN, rather than comparing only against fixed numerical solvers.

Practical considerations are treated seriously: the appendices report training-set-size sensitivity, cross-dataset transfer, adversarial-loss sensitivity, training time, memory consumption, inference time, and extensive hyperparameters.
The method adds essentially no inference-time overhead relative to standard solvers with the same number of model evaluations, making the reported quality gains practically meaningful.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than fundamental. The main ingredients—overparameterized linear multistep updates, residual correction of an existing solver, sampler distillation, and adversarial training—are individually established ideas; the contribution is primarily their effective combination.

The parameterization ablation is not sufficiently diagnostic. Table 3 compares the complete proposed parameterization against one reimplemented S4S variant, but does not separately isolate all-history states, all-history velocities, additive theoretical guidance, schedule learning, and evaluation-time corrections. Moreover, the reimplemented S4S results in Table 3 are substantially worse than the S4S-Alt results in Table 2, weakening the claimed attribution.

Benefits from adversarial training are concentrated mainly at the smallest NFE. GAS is nearly identical to or sometimes worse than GS at larger NFEs, including several ImageNet and MS-COCO settings. Thus, claims of systematic improvement should be narrowed to difficult low-NFE regimes.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on FID, without repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, precision/recall or density/coverage metrics. This is especially limiting for an adversarial objective, where improved FID need not establish preserved diversity or absence of mode dropping.

The claimed improvement in fine-grained detail is supported primarily by a small qualitative figure. Perceptual studies or suitable fidelity metrics are missing; for text-to-image generation, there is also no CLIP score, prompt-alignment evaluation, or human assessment.

Comparison fairness is imperfect because many baseline numbers are imported from prior papers and may involve different implementations, teachers, losses, training budgets, and hardware. Some strongest S4S comparisons are explicitly marked as using a different-quality teacher, while training-time comparisons mix A100, H100, and TPU measurements.

The approach still requires separate optimization for each model and generally each NFE budget, backpropagation through the full sampler, and up to roughly 66 GB of reported training memory. These costs temper its presentation as a lightweight acceleration technique.

The manuscript states that code is available but provides an empty link in the submitted version. Despite detailed hyperparameters and pseudocode, absent code and missing seed or run-variance information limit reproducibility.

strengths: The generalized solver parameterization is simple, computationally lightweight at inference, and compatible with pretrained diffusion models without modifying their networks.
The reported low-NFE gains are substantial in several settings, particularly at 4–6 function evaluations on CIFAR-10, FFHQ, AFHQv2, LSUN Bedroom, and ImageNet.
The evaluation spans six datasets, including pixel-space, latent-space, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation.
The paper provides useful efficiency measurements, extensive hyperparameters, dataset-size studies, transfer experiments, and qualitative comparisons.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is modest: the method combines an overparameterized linear multistep update, additive corrections to an existing solver, and a standard adversarial objective. There is no theoretical analysis of consistency, stability, or when the learned coefficients should generalize.

The comparisons are not sufficiently controlled. Many baseline numbers are copied from prior papers, some use teachers with materially different FID, and runtime comparisons mix hardware and protocols. Consequently, the tables do not isolate improvements due to the proposed method.

For pixel-space GAS, pretrained CIFAR-10 or FFHQ R3GAN discriminators introduce target-domain data and prior training unavailable to solver-only baselines. There is no random-initialization or matched-compute ablation, so the adversarial gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed training formulation.

Evaluation relies almost entirely on FID without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, precision/recall, or other diversity measures. Text-to-image experiments omit prompt-alignment metrics and human evaluation. Random samples and low FID do not substantiate the claim that mode collapse is absent.

The claim of uniformly superior performance is contradicted by the tables: S4S is equal or better in some AFHQv2 high-NFE settings, GAS sometimes offers negligible or negative improvement over GS, and the Stable Diffusion student remains worse than its teacher.

The ablations do not separately establish the value of all-history states, all-history velocities, timestep optimization, decoupled evaluation times, and theoretical initialization. Alternative guiding solvers and discriminator choices are also not studied.

Reproducibility is weakened by inconsistent Stable Diffusion training-set descriptions (1000 samples in the main table caption versus 1400/5000 in the appendix), a blank code URL, and pseudocode that describes an individual update without a complete executable training procedure.

Generalization evidence is narrow, covering only transfer between closely related FFHQ and AFHQv2 models. The method otherwise requires separate optimization for each model and NFE budget, and its backpropagation cost grows substantially with model scale and step count.

strengths: Clear and practically relevant contribution: the generalized multistep parameterization combines learned coefficients with theoretically derived initialization, while adversarial training targets artifacts that regression-based solver distillation can retain.

Broad evaluation across six datasets, covering pixel-space, latent-space, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation. The strongest gains are substantial in the challenging 4-NFE regime, such as FFHQ and AFHQv2.
The paper includes useful ablations and efficiency analyses covering adversarial training, convergence, dataset size, loss weight, cross-dataset transfer, memory, and inference time.

The method preserves the original diffusion network and adds essentially no inference-time overhead beyond the chosen number of function evaluations. Experimental settings and pseudocode are described in considerable detail.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate: the method mainly combines an overparameterized linear multistep solver, theoretically guided initialization, and established adversarial distillation techniques. Its value is primarily empirical rather than a fundamentally new solver principle.

The central parameterization comparison is not fully convincing. The reproduced S4S variant in Table 3 performs much worse than the published S4S-Alt results in Table 2, and simultaneously changing solver order, coefficient representation, and theoretical guidance does not isolate which design choice produces the gain.

Results are reported without repeated runs, confidence intervals, or FID uncertainty. Several claimed improvements at higher NFEs are only a few hundredths of a FID point and may not be statistically meaningful; GAS also sometimes matches or slightly underperforms GS.

Evidence for improved fine-grained perceptual quality relies mainly on FID and a limited set of qualitative examples, some explicitly selected to maximize GS–GAS differences. Text-to-image experiments omit complementary measures such as prompt-alignment or human-preference evaluation.

The learned solver has no consistency or stability analysis, and the validity constraints on the corrected model-evaluation times are insufficiently specified. Training-time comparisons also mix different accelerator types and are therefore only approximate.

strengths: The generalized solver is a clear and useful extension of learned multistep diffusion solvers: it combines all prior states and velocities with additive corrections to theoretically derived DPM-Solver++ coefficients.

The empirical study is broad, covering six datasets, pixel- and latent-space models, conditional generation, and Stable Diffusion across several low-NFE settings. GS/GAS generally improves substantially over training-free solvers and often over LD3 and S4S.

The paper includes valuable ablations of theoretical guidance, solver parameterization, adversarial-loss formulation and weight, dataset size, training dynamics, diversity, memory, and inference time. In particular, the controlled parameterization comparisons and theory-guidance ablation support the main design choice.

The method is lightweight relative to full model distillation, leaves the diffusion model frozen, and adds essentially no inference-time overhead. The reported data and training requirements are practically attractive.
The presentation is generally clear, and the appendix supplies pseudocode, optimization settings, teacher configurations, qualitative samples, and resource measurements.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental: additive corrections around a standard solver and adversarially augmented distillation are individually established ideas. The paper provides limited theoretical analysis of why the highly overparameterized history-based update should generalize or remain numerically stable.

Comparison fairness is imperfect. Many headline baseline numbers are imported from prior papers rather than reproduced under an identical teacher, data, implementation, and hardware setup; some S4S latent results are explicitly marked incomparable. This weakens the claim of systematic superiority.

There is a material inconsistency in the Stable Diffusion protocol: Table 2 states that training uses 1,000 MS-COCO samples, whereas Appendix D.4.3 specifies 1,400 samples for GS and 5,000 for GAS. Table 18 additionally refers to 30,000 prompts without clearly separating evaluation and training generation. This should be corrected for reproducibility.

Results are reported without multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Several high-NFE improvements are extremely small or reverse direction, and GAS provides only modest gains on Stable Diffusion while sometimes underperforming GS or even its one-step-larger teacher.

Evidence for enhanced fine-grained detail and text-to-image quality rests mainly on FID and selected qualitative examples. Human preference, prompt-alignment, or complementary perceptual evaluations are absent; FID alone does not fully support these claims.

Training must generally be repeated for every model and target NFE. Cross-dataset transfer is demonstrated only between closely related 64x64 animal/face models, while unconstrained evaluation-time offsets lack monotonicity or range guarantees despite an observed timestep exceeding the nominal domain.
The claimed code link is empty in the manuscript, so the implementation was not available for verification despite reliance on a nontrivial custom S4S reimplementation.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving diffusion ODE sampling in low-NFE regimes without updating the pretrained diffusion model.
The generalized solver parameterization is simple and reasonably motivated, combining theoretical solver coefficients with learned additive corrections and access to prior states and velocities.

The empirical study covers six datasets across pixel-space, latent-space, class-conditional, and text-to-image settings, with useful ablations on theoretical guidance, adversarial loss, dataset size, transfer, memory, and runtime.
Several low-NFE results are promising, particularly on FFHQ, AFHQv2, and LSUN, and the authors explicitly evaluate diversity and mode-collapse concerns.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. Learning solver coefficients and schedules is closely related to LD3 and S4S, while adding a standard adversarial objective to regression-based distillation is well established. The paper does not provide a theoretical result explaining when its enlarged, unconstrained solver is stable or generalizes.

The headline claim of outperforming existing methods across all datasets is not supported cleanly. GAS sometimes provides negligible gains or degrades GS at higher NFE, does not beat the reported S4S result on ImageNet at NFE=4, and several S4S comparisons are explicitly marked incomparable because their teacher configurations differ.

Baseline fairness is a major concern. Many numbers are copied from prior papers under potentially different teachers, losses, hardware, or implementations. The authors reimplement S4S because no official implementation is available, but the reimplementation performs dramatically worse than the published variant in some settings, making the central parameterization comparison difficult to trust.

The evaluation relies overwhelmingly on FID without confidence intervals, repeated runs, or statistical significance. Small differences such as 2.17 versus 2.18 are therefore not persuasive. The claimed improvement in fine-grained detail is supported mainly by selected qualitative examples rather than a targeted perceptual study or quantitative detail metric.

The text-to-image evaluation is incomplete: it reports only FID, without CLIP-based alignment, human preference, prompt-following, or compositional metrics. Training on only 1,000 COCO samples also raises overfitting and generalization questions that are not adequately investigated.

The adversarial objective matches marginal teacher distributions using unpaired noises, so it does not directly support the stated claim of preserving teacher-specific fine details. It can trade correspondence for realism, as the paper itself observes through worse distillation losses and outputs farther from their paired teachers.

The learned coefficients and model-evaluation times are largely unconstrained. The appendix admits an evaluation timestep outside the training range, yet offers no systematic stability, robustness, or failure analysis. Separate optimization for each dataset, model, and NFE further limits practicality.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the abstract says 'Code is available at' but supplies no link. Despite extensive hyperparameter reporting, exact implementation and baseline reproduction cannot be independently verified from the submission.

Overall, the paper contains substantial experimentation and plausible improvements, but the incremental contribution, questionable comparison protocol, narrow metrics, and unsupported broad claims make the evidence insufficient for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant approach: a flexible all-history multistep sampler initialized with theoretically derived DPM-Solver++ coefficients, followed by lightweight coefficient and timestep optimization.

The evaluation is unusually broad for solver optimization, spanning six datasets and pixel-space, latent-space, class-conditional, and text-to-image settings. Improvements are particularly compelling at low NFE, such as FFHQ, AFHQv2, LSUN-Bedroom, and ImageNet at 4–6 evaluations.

The ablations substantively support the main design choices. Theoretical guidance substantially improves FID; adversarial training improves low-NFE FID and visible artifacts; and additional studies cover GAN loss choice, adversarial weight, training-set size, convergence, memory, inference time, and diversity.

The method is computationally attractive relative to full model distillation: it freezes the diffusion model, trains comparatively few sampler parameters in hours, and introduces essentially no measured inference-time overhead beyond the fixed NFE budget.

The presentation is generally clear, with useful pseudocode, detailed hyperparameters, teacher configurations, and extensive qualitative examples. weaknesses: The methodological novelty is moderate rather than major. The two central ingredients—learning solver coefficients around a theoretical initialization and adding an adversarial loss to regression-based distillation—are natural extensions of prior solver optimization and adversarial diffusion-distillation work.

The strongest claim of outperforming all prior methods is not fully controlled. Many baseline numbers are imported from other papers, some use materially different teachers, and the authors’ S4S comparison relies on their own implementation because no official implementation is available. The paper itself marks several latent-space S4S results as not directly comparable.

The text-to-image evaluation is incomplete: it reports only FID, without CLIP-based alignment, human preference, or other prompt-fidelity measurements. FID alone cannot establish that perceptual improvements preserve text conditioning, especially when some students obtain a lower FID than their own teachers.

The paper provides no numerical-analysis account of consistency, stability, or behavior outside the trained model/NFE regime. Because the parameterization freely combines every prior state and velocity, empirical performance does not establish that the learned object remains a robust ODE solver.

GAS provides clear gains mainly in the most aggressive low-NFE settings and is often tied with, or slightly worse than, GS at higher NFE. Its added training time and adversarial complexity therefore have a narrower benefit than some of the paper’s language suggests.

Reproducibility is weakened by a missing code URL ('Code is available at.'), minor numerical inconsistencies across tables, and inconsistent descriptions of the MS-COCO training-set size (the main table says 1,000, whereas the appendix specifies 1,400 for GS and 5,000 for GAS).
